title: Git Rebase vs Merge: Complete Handbook
summary: Quick revision notes on how rebase and merge each shape history, fast-forward vs merge commits, interactive rebase, the golden rule, pull --rebase, and when to pick which.

chapters.title: Rebase vs Merge: The Mental Model
points: Merge joins two branches by creating a new commit with two parents; both histories are preserved exactly as they happened
Rebase replays your branch's commits one by one on top of another base, producing new commits with new SHAs
Merge is non-destructive and adds history; rebase rewrites history and gives a linear one
Rebased commits are copies: same diff and message, different parent and hash, so the old commits are orphaned
Mental model: merge = 'tie the two lines together'; rebase = 'pretend I branched from the latest tip'

chapters.title: Fast-Forward vs Merge Commit
points: Fast-forward: if the target branch has no new commits, git just moves the branch pointer forward; no merge commit is created
Merge commit (true merge): when both branches diverged, git creates a commit with two parents
git merge --no-ff forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible, keeping the feature branch visible in the graph
git merge --ff-only refuses to merge unless it can fast-forward; it fails safely on divergence
git log --oneline --graph --all shows the shape: a straight line means fast-forward or rebase, a diamond means a merge commit

chapters.title: Rebase in Practice and Conflicts
points: git switch feature && git rebase main replays feature's commits onto the tip of main
Conflicts are resolved per commit: fix files, git add, then git rebase --continue
git rebase --abort restores the branch to its state before the rebase; git rebase --skip drops the current commit
git reflog is the safety net: find the pre-rebase SHA and git reset --hard to it to undo a bad rebase
After rebasing a branch already pushed, update it with git push --force-with-lease, never plain --force

chapters.title: Interactive Rebase: Squash, Reword, Drop
points: git rebase -i HEAD~N opens a todo list of the last N commits, oldest first, to edit before replay
pick keeps a commit; reword (r) keeps its changes but lets you edit the message
squash (s) melts a commit into the previous one and combines messages; fixup (f) does the same but discards the message
drop (d) or deleting the line removes the commit; reordering lines reorders commits
git commit --fixup <sha> followed by git rebase -i --autosquash auto-arranges fixup commits

chapters.title: The Golden Rule and pull --rebase
points: Golden rule: never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch others build on, because it rewrites hashes and forces everyone else into painful reconciliation
Rebasing your own unpushed or private feature branch is safe
git pull = fetch + merge, which creates noisy merge commits when local and remote diverge; git pull --rebase = fetch + rebase, replaying your local commits on top of origin
git config --global pull.rebase true makes rebase the default pull behavior; pull.ff only makes pulls fail rather than create a merge
Never rebase main or master; if someone already rebased a shared branch, fix with git pull --rebase and check git reflog

chapters.title: When to Use Which: Cheat Sheet
points: Use rebase to tidy your private branch and update it from main before opening a PR (linear, clean history)
Use merge to integrate shared or long-lived branches and when preserving the true history matters
Squash merge collapses a PR into one commit on main: clean history but loses individual commit detail
Cheat sheet: git rebase main | git rebase -i HEAD~N | git rebase --continue/--abort/--skip | git merge --no-ff/--ff-only | git push --force-with-lease | git pull --rebase
Decision rule: private and unpushed means rebase; public and shared means merge
